A: Coronal chest CT panel from a case report of Caplan syndrome; the in-text description specifically reports bilateral multiple subpleural nodules on chest CT, a recognized pulmonary manifestation of Caplan syndrome. in_text_mentions: On initial physical examination, he was febrile (37.9°C). Fine crackles were noted on auscultation over the right chest. The upper limb joints showed a restricted range of motion due to pain. Chest CT revealed bilateral, multiple subpleural nodules with air bronchograms, predominantly in the upper lobes, along with segmental bronchial wall thickening. The previous TB cavitary lesion located in the left upper lobe had recurred (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E of CT-guided lung biopsy from a patient with Caplan syndrome; shows a nodular granulomatous/fibrotic lesion with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate and carbon pigment, though the in-text notes the full zonal architecture of a classic Caplan nodule was not captured, so typicality is variant and confidence moderate. B: H&E lung biopsy panel showing a rounded necrobiotic granulomatous nodule with palisading histiocytes and central eosinophilic material in a biopsy-confirmed Caplan syndrome case; the caption/in-text note incomplete zonal architecture, hence variant. C: H&E of peribronchial (hilar) lymph node tissue from the Caplan syndrome case showing fibrotic/dust-related change; no specific vocabulary finding is captioned for this panel and the change is non-specific, so confidence is low. D: Histology of peribronchial lymph node with abundant black carbon pigment, corresponding to the in-text description of abundant carbon dust...

in_text_mentions: n histopathological confirmation. It revealed alveolar wall fibroplasia and chronic inflammation with infiltration of numerous lymphocytes and plasmocytes, as well as abundant carbon dust deposition (Figure 3). Polarized microscopy and special stains (hexamine silver stain, acid-fast stain, and periodic acid–Schiff stain) were negative. No evidence of tumor or microorganism was found. Notably, the full zonal architecture of a classic Caplan nodule was not captured due to the limited biopsy size, and the central zone could not be fully evaluated microscopically. panels.rationale: Single-panel H&E histology of the patient's transbronchial biopsy showing a necrobiotic/necrotic lung nodule, described in the caption as the necrobiotic nodule of the right upper lobe lesion in an article titled "Caplan's Syndrome with a twist." The finding maps to the rheumatoid/necrobiotic nodule histology vocabulary item, though the caption emphasizes necrotic tissue with silica crystals (silico-anthracotic nodule) rather than a textbook palisading granuloma, so attribution confidence is moderate.
panels.attribution_text: Deepak and Kenaa. Caplan's Syndrome with a twist.. International journal of clinical case reports and reviews : open access 2020. doi:10.31579/2690-4861/007. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3:.
panels.figure_caption: Pathology of the necrobiotic nodule from the transbronchial biopsy of the Right upper lobe nodule.
in_text_mentions: Pulmonary function test (PFT) revealed mild obstructive ventilator defect with FEV1/FVC 66%, FEV1 of 3.13L, 94% predicted. He underwent bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsies of the right upper lobe nodules. Pathology revealed a necrotic tissue (Figure 3) with central silica crystals visualized under polarized light which was consistent with silico-anthracotic nodules. The biopsies were negative for malignancy. There was no evidence of infection on bronchoalveolar lavage. His AFB and fungal cultures were also negative.
